video_title: Ukraine & Russia's War Budgets (2027) - Pressure, Priorities & Economic Pain Points
gist: Perun walks through Russia's and Ukraine's draft 2027 war budgets: Russia at a record ~$200B defense with a 3.2% deficit funded by domestic borrowing and non-military cuts, Ukraine at ~44% of GDP defense and a 15% deficit reliant on European loans. He argues the ~2:1 spending ratio is unchanged, both budgets will be revised up, and the swing factors are oil, Ukrainian strikes (refineries, grain, data centers), winter bombing and aid politics.

insights.claim: Russia is set to approve a post-Soviet record defense budget of roughly $200B for 2027, about 27% above 2026, with projected spending jumping from under 14 trillion to over 17 trillion rubles, reversing March 2026 plans for flat or falling defense outlays.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Russian planners expected defense relief and energy windfall; got only the energy half, so the war economy is not easing.

insights.claim: Russian budget planners expected energy revenue up and defense spending down; they got about one third right: oil prices far exceed forecasts, but defense spending is rising, and volumes (hit by Ukrainian strikes) are the offset on oil income.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: High prices without export volumes is a weaker windfall than headline oil prices imply.

insights.claim: Rising Russian defense costs reflect depletion of Soviet-era stockpiles: with fewer refurbishable tanks and artillery and larger recruit bonuses, Russia must spend more each year just to achieve the same military output.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Structural cost inflation in Russian defense means flat budgets equal shrinking capability.
insights.quote: over time, Russian defense spending had to increase just to achieve the same results less spending might have achieved earlier

insights.claim: The Russian economy has passed through three acts: 2022 shock plus stimulus, 2023-24 adaptation and growth with high export prices and shadow-fleet rerouting, and a 2025-26 stagnation phase with persistent inflation, rising debt and diminishing returns on wartime stimulus.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Use energy price, growth, war spend and kinetic-sanction damage as the four variables to date regime changes.

insights.claim: Russian growth forecasts are weak: below 1% in 2026 and about 1.4% in 2027 per Russian figures, closer to 0.7% in 2027 per the World Bank.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: A 27% defense increase on a near-zero-growth base means crowding out of the rest of the economy.

insights.claim: Russia is financing the budget through trade-offs rather than strain: more domestic borrowing, cuts to non-military items, higher taxes and fines, windfall taxes on mining and metals (about 200B rubles per year 2027-29), and voluntary donations from wealthy businessmen (about 1% of 2026 spending, reportedly around $5.6B).
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Fiscal levers are being pulled across the board, sacrificing economic future to sustain the war now.

insights.claim: Russia's 2026 deficit target crept from 1.6% of GDP to 3% to 3.2%; this is low by global standards (US about 6%), but the speed of increase, high servicing costs and lack of international market access make it a watch item.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: The binding constraint is who can buy ruble debt, not deficit size.

insights.claim: Russia plans about $92B of ruble bond issuance in 2027 (roughly $1.8B per week) and already has trouble at bond auctions at a 3.2% deficit; scaling to 9-10% would likely need coercive measures such as 'voluntelling' people to buy war bonds.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Weak auctions or sharply higher yields are the early indicator of forced financing or cuts.
insights.quote: historically speaking, you'd probably be looking at more coercive funding measures like voluntelling people to buy war bonds

insights.claim: Over 90% of Russian government debt is held domestically, so any debt problem would fall on Russians, while sanctions block foreign borrowing.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Debt stress is a domestic banking and household problem, not an external default risk.

insights.claim: Russian regions are cutting death-in-action payouts to fund rising recruit costs, e.g. Bashkortostan from 2 million to 100,000 rubles, Ulyanovsk from 1 million to 50,000, Orenburg cancelling from July 1; meanwhile recruiter finder fees (about 400,000 rubles in one region) are creating press-gang style corruption.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Recruitment is getting costlier and more coercive; August 2026 contract signings were about 1,000 per day, roughly 20% lower year on year.

insights.claim: Russia has non-Ukraine defense burdens (nuclear modernization with a 9-year high in deployed warheads, expired last nuclear treaty, global navy, NATO borders including Finland), so its larger budget buys less relative advantage than the ratio suggests.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Raw 2:1 budget ratio overstates Russia's usable edge in Ukraine.

insights.claim: Russian equipment stocks are nearly exhausted: of 7,216 tanks seen in storage before February 2022 only about 150 remain in decent condition (about 1,400 including poor), with all T-90s and nearly all T-80Bs gone, forcing new builds and repair of front-line returns.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Soviet inheritance as a free resource is ending; costs of new production will rise.

insights.claim: Russia is polarizing equipment: cheaper ATVs, buggies and motorcycles at one end, and increasingly expensive upgraded systems like jet-powered Geran drones at the other, which pushes the budget up further.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Expect Russian budget upward revisions as unit costs climb.

insights.claim: Ukraine's 2027 plan puts security and defense spending at about 44% of GDP per the KSC Institute, above US 1943 levels, and just over two thirds of every government dollar goes to the war, versus Russia's roughly 6-8% of GDP.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Ukraine dedicates far more of a smaller pie; this explains why the war stays close despite economic disparity.
insights.quote: Ukraine is going to be at about 44%

insights.claim: Ukraine's Ministry of Defense gets about $80B in 2027 (up about 3%), $88.5B including National Guard and Border Guard, and $104.1B total security and defense, which alone exceeds Russia's 2021 defense budget in real terms.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Ukraine's outlay is large in absolute terms, not just proportionally.

insights.claim: Ukraine's deficit is projected at 12.4% of GDP in 2026 and 15% in 2027, and would be far higher without foreign grants; roughly 57% of 2027 government revenue is expected from foreign sources.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: The Ukrainian theory of victory rests on sustained external financing.

insights.claim: Ukraine can borrow roughly three times as much as Russia for a similar interest burden because softer loans bring its weighted borrowing cost to about 5.12% versus 16%+ on Russian bonds; unsanctioned Russia at a 14.2% deficit would add about $282B a year, enough to raise its defense budget 140%.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Sanctions and credit access, not GDP, are what hold the resource gap near parity.
insights.quote: Ukraine can borrow about three times as much as Russia can while acrewing about the same interest burden

insights.claim: The European Union support loan is expected to deliver about $52B to Ukraine in 2027, of which $36.8B for defense and $15.4B for general needs.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: European financing is the load-bearing element of Ukraine's 2027 plan.

insights.claim: Ukraine's economy is still growing (1.8% in 2025, 1.6% in 2026, 1.3% projected 2027) with about 8% inflation, largely due to wartime spending and foreign injections; but these projections predate Odesa attacks, the Black Sea mutual denial and any winter bombing damage.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Ukrainian macro assumptions carry downside risk.

insights.claim: Ukraine's defense budget is likely squeezed: an illustrative build shows about $23B for drones and strike systems plus $38B personnel (up nearly $10B) leaving only about $28B of an $89B pool for armor, munitions, air defense and sustainment, so overspend or frontloading of European funds is likely.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Expect Ukrainian budget overruns and frontloading that leaves a hole in late 2027.
insights.quote: I think it might be even more likely the Ukrainians overrun their spending target than the Russians do theirs

insights.claim: Ukraine claims drone capacity of 10 million per year in 2026 with a 20 million goal for 2027, plus about 50,000 ground drones in 2026, and Russia claims about 7,000 Ukrainian long-range drones monthly (roughly $6.3B a year at $75,000 each).
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Ukraine is building its budget around drones as a comparative advantage.

insights.claim: Donated Western equipment (e.g. free older Gripen C/D aircraft from 2027, German-funded MAR self-propelled guns from 2027) does not appear in the defense budget, so Ukraine's real resource position is better than budget lines show.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Aid in kind frees the Ukrainian budget for drones and long-range strike.

insights.claim: Reported procurement tensions under former defense minister Fedorov included tender-based requirements procurement, favoring long-range shells, and pausing new orders for domestic armored vehicles and the 2S22 Bohdana, with producers saying no new state orders for nine months.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Ukraine is reprioritizing scarce funds, with possible idle domestic capacity.

insights.claim: Russia, formerly the world's second largest diesel exporter, has not exported diesel for months due to a domestic shortfall and an export ban, so high global diesel prices bring it little benefit and it has even been importing.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Ukrainian refinery strikes are neutralizing Russia's price windfall by cutting product volumes.

insights.claim: The reported US-Russia deal to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel is small (300,000 tons in October, 500,000 in November, under one day of US consumption) and cannot move the market, but gives Moscow leverage to blame Ukrainian refinery strikes for US fuel prices and press Kyiv to stop.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: The real risk is signaling and pressure on Ukraine's energy strike campaign, not barrels.

insights.claim: Because diesel is a globally commodified good, rerouting Russian cargoes to the US does not change global supply; only Russian production matters, so repair of refineries (which Ukraine hits) would do more for US prices than sanctions relief.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: An energy ceasefire (Ukraine reportedly open to refinery-for-grid swap) would raise Russian output and move futures; sanctions are the wrong lever.

insights.claim: Oil prices are far above what the Russian budget needs, due to the Middle East war and suppressed Iranian supply, but whether Russia profits depends on Gulf supply routes and on Ukrainian strikes limiting export volumes.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Watch Middle East supply and Ukrainian strikes as the two oil-revenue swing factors.

themes.theme: Black Sea, Grain and New Target Sets

insights.claim: The Black Sea is in near mutual denial: shipping from Ukrainian ports has collapsed and so has Russian traffic from Novorossiysk, with a double-digit percentage of world grain supply reportedly affected.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Both grain exporters are hurt; watch wheat flows and prices.

insights.claim: Russian wheat exports are forecast at about 5.6 million tons in July-September 2026 versus 11.3 million a year earlier, farmers are selling at 5-6 thousand rubles per ton against 11-13 thousand cost, and the 2027 harvest could be 10-12% smaller.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Expect Russian state intervention in agriculture (rail priority already) with spillovers to other sectors.
insights.quote: a 2027 harvest that might be 10 to 12% smaller than 2026

insights.claim: Ukraine's targeting expands to new economic pain points each year (refineries 2022-25, e-commerce warehouses 2025, data centers in October 2026), and Russia has had to bail out affected sectors such as e-commerce and coal.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: The other side gets a vote; budget plans can be undone by new target categories.

insights.claim: Russian digital infrastructure is more vulnerable than Ukraine's: Ukraine moved critical government and banking data to Amazon cloud in 2022, while Russia's sovereignty approach concentrates large data centers (e.g. a 49 MW Yandex facility hit) that are costly to replace amid a global bidding war.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Russian data centers are expensive, mostly in air-defended Moscow, but a rebuild competes with the AI buildout for equipment.

themes.theme: Winter Risk, Aid Politics and Outlook

insights.claim: Ukraine enters winter with worse air defense than in 2025: Russia has jet drones, cruise and ballistic missiles, last year's energy damage is not fully repaired, and anti-ballistic interceptors were depleted by Middle East consumption.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Winter strikes are the main near-term unknown for the Ukrainian 2027 economy.

insights.claim: Past Russian infrastructure campaigns did not push Ukraine back into recession or stop growth in military production, and Ukraine's budget gap for late 2026 and early 2027 is patched partly by accelerating already-pledged aid.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Civilian pain does not translate cleanly into lower military output.
insights.quote: forcing pensioners to freeze in their flats doesn't necessarily stop the guys in the workshop putting together drones

insights.claim: European elections are a key 2027 risk, with France's April election highlighted; Russia's economic victory theory needs Ukraine cut off from aid, while Ukraine's needs aid sustained until Russia accepts a ceasefire.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Aid-continuity politics, not budgets, may decide the balance.

insights.claim: Neither budget is likely to shift the resource balance in 2027, and both are likely to be revised upward; with the funding ratio near 2:1 and unchanged from 2026, neither side gets decisive economic advantage.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Expect continued attrition with both sides budgeting for more of the same.
insights.quote: both sides might well be hoping for the best, but budgeting for more of the attritional same
